Female Lesser sirens reach a snout-vent length of approximately 15.0 centimeters  by their first year of age, while males of the same cohort attain a notably larger size of about 18.5 centimeters . This divergence in early growth trajectories between the sexes foreshadows the pronounced sexual size dimorphism characteristic of the species. Under captive conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan approaches 25.7 years [am = 25.7 years], an exceptional longevity for a paedomorphic amphibian that likely reflects a slow metabolic pace and the absence of the energetic costs associated with metamorphosis. In the field, estimates of longevity are more variable, but the oldest individuals recovered from mark-recapture studies approach a similar duration, suggesting that the species' extended life span is a genuine feature of its life history rather than an artifact of laboratory rearing conditions. The largest females attain a maximum adult size of 25.5 centimeters [Li = 25.5 centimeters] in snout-vent length, whereas males achieve a substantially greater ultimate snout-vent length of 31.5 centimeters [Li = 31.5 centimeters], underscoring the role of male-male competition or fecundity selection in driving these divergent body size optima.

At the onset of reproductive activity, females reach puberty when they have achieved a snout-vent length of 15.0 centimeters [Lp = 15.0 centimeters], a size that corresponds closely to their first-year growth and suggests that most females are capable of breeding within their first year of life if environmental conditions permit. Males, in contrast, begin gametogenesis at a larger body size, with puberty recorded at a snout-vent length of 19.0 centimeters [Lp = 19.0 centimeters], a threshold that may delay their first reproductive opportunity relative to females. Among related sirenid species, these size thresholds are comparatively modest, reflecting the paedomorphic and energetically conservative lifestyle of Siren intermedia. Breeding occurs once per year [F_R_i = once per year], with females depositing a single clutch of eggs annually. Clutch size ranges from 120 to 130 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 120 to 130 eggs per clutch], representing a substantial reproductive output given the relatively small body size of the female. The combination of moderate fecundity and low annual reproductive frequency suggests that Siren intermedia relies on high offspring survival rather than iteroparity to maintain stable population numbers.

Neonates emerge from the egg at a minute wet weight of just 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a figure that aligns well with the species' small egg diameter of approximately 3 millimeters. At a developmental temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at birth is 35 days [ab = 35 days], indicating a protracted embryonic period typical of paedomorphic salamanders inhabiting cool, thermally stable aquatic environments. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae are entirely lecithotrophic for the first several weeks, relying exclusively on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding on small aquatic invertebrates and detritus. The growth trajectory from this minute birth mass to the adult body size is steep but prolonged, reflecting the species' capacity for indeterminate growth in an environment where food resources may be seasonally abundant. In captivity, individuals fed ad libitum and maintained at warmer temperatures attain adult mass much more rapidly, but the maximum recorded adult wet weight under natural conditions is approximately 266 grams [Wwi = approximately 266 grams], a figure that underscores the siren's ability to accumulate substantial biomass over decades of continued growth.

The maximum reproductive rate under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, a stable 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is derived from the annual deposition of a single clutch of 120 to 130 eggs. This modest rate, far lower than that of many anurans or metamorphosing salamanders, is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by a strictly aquatic, paedomorphic life history in which somatic growth and maintenance take priority over rapid gamete production. Intraspecific variation in reproductive output is positively correlated with female body size, as larger, older females tend to produce clutches at the upper end of the observed range. Studies comparing reproductive investment across Siren populations indicate that clutch size is also influenced by local temperature regimes, with cooler environments typically associated with somewhat smaller clutches. The annual reproductive schedule is tightly coupled to the seasonal hydroperiod, with ovulation and egg deposition occurring in late winter or early spring when water levels are high and food availability for newly hatched larvae is maximal. This phenological match ensures that the energetically demanding yolk provisioning phase coincides with peak prey abundance.

Growth rings in the vertebral centra and annuli in the otoliths of Siren intermedia indicate that the oldest individuals in wild populations achieve lifespans approaching 25.7 years [am = 25.7 years] when mean annual water temperatures are near 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a conclusion corroborated by long-term captive records. This exceptional longevity, more than double that of most similarly sized amphibians, is likely facilitated by the species' low resting metabolic rate, its paedomorphic retention of gills and lateral line systems that reduce the costs of pulmonary ventilation, and its ability to withstand prolonged hypoxia during aestivation in drying ponds. By the time neonates emerge from the egg mass at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at birth is 35 days [ab = 35 days], a developmental interval that is extended relative to many anurans but typical of urodeles that invest heavily in yolk provisioning. The initial wet weight of these hatchlings is approximately 0.0141 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0141 grams], a tenth or less of the hatchling mass reported for many large ambystomatid salamanders. This minute birth mass imposes a narrow window for first feeding success, as the small larvae are vulnerable to starvation if planktonic prey is not immediately abundant following yolk-sac resorption.
